note: The ten priority topics. Each has a current-charter page even where historical comparison data does not exist yet. charter_text stays null until the actual charter language is obtained. Never fill it with a paraphrase.

records.name: Recall
records.what_is_it: Recall is a process where residents collect signatures to force an election on whether an elected official should be removed from office before their term ends.
records.can_residents_do_it: Almost certainly yes in some form. Texas home rule charters generally include recall, and Copperas Cove is a home rule city. The exact rules have not been obtained.
records.charter_location: Article III. Sec. 3.13 Power to recall, 3.14 Results of recall election, 3.15 Limitation on recall, 3.16 Public hearing, 3.17 Ballots in recall election. Sec. 3.18 is Reserved.
records.has_changed: Unknown. No recall-related measure appears in the 2021 or 2023 records we hold.
records.why_it_matters: Recall is the only way residents can remove an elected official between elections. The signature threshold and the time limits decide whether that power is realistic or symbolic.

records.name: Initiative
records.what_is_it: Initiative is a process where residents collect signatures to put a proposed ordinance on the ballot, so voters can pass a law the council has not passed.
records.can_residents_do_it: Yes. The charter provides for initiative petitions. This is confirmed indirectly because the 2021 ballot included a measure changing what a signer must write on an initiative petition.
records.requirements: A signer must include either a date of birth or a voter registration number, not both, if Measure F passed in 2021. The number of signatures required has not been obtained.
records.charter_location: Article III. Sec. 3.06 Power of initiative, with 3.08 Requirements of petition, 3.09 Filing, examination and certification of petition, 3.11 Council consideration and submission to voters, 3.12 Ballot form and results of elections.
records.has_changed: Yes. Measure F on the November 2, 2021 ballot changed the signature information requirement. The outcome of that vote has not been confirmed.
records.why_it_matters: Initiative is how residents pass something the council will not. The signature threshold is what makes it usable or unusable.

records.name: Referendum
records.what_is_it: Referendum is a process where residents collect signatures to force a public vote on an ordinance the council already passed, so voters can overturn it.
records.can_residents_do_it: Yes. The charter provides for referendum petitions, confirmed indirectly by the 2021 measure on petition signature requirements.
records.requirements: Same signature information rule as initiative under Measure F. The signature count and the deadline after an ordinance passes have not been obtained.
records.charter_location: Article III. Sec. 3.07 Power of referendum, with 3.08, 3.09, 3.10 Effect of certification of referendum petition, 3.11 and 3.12.
records.has_changed: Yes, in the same 2021 measure as initiative.
records.why_it_matters: Referendum is the check on an unpopular ordinance. The deadline matters as much as the signature count, because the clock usually starts the day the ordinance passes.

records.name: Charter amendments
records.what_is_it: A charter amendment is a change to the city's charter, which functions somewhat like a local constitution.
records.can_residents_do_it: Residents are the only ones who can approve a charter amendment. A charter amendment requires approval by a majority of the qualified voters of the city who vote at an election held for that purpose. The Texas Attorney General has opined that a home rule charter cannot provide for amendment by ordinance alone.
records.requirements: Majority of voters voting at an election held for that purpose, under Texas Local Government Code sec. 9.005(a). State law also limits how often a city may order a charter amendment election; the current statute text has not been pulled.
records.charter_location: Article XI. Sec. 11.18 Amending the charter.
records.has_changed: The state rule is state law, not charter language, so it changes in Austin rather than locally.
records.why_it_matters: Only voters can approve a charter change, but the City Council orders the election and sets the ballot language. That means the council decides which proposals residents get to vote on at all. Both halves of that sentence are true at once.

records.name: City elections and who can run
records.what_is_it: The charter sets when city elections happen, how ballots are prepared, and who is qualified to run for mayor or council.
records.can_residents_do_it: Residents vote in city elections and may run for office if they meet the qualifications.
records.requirements: Measure A in 2021 proposed requiring a candidate to be 18 by the first day of the term, registered to vote by the filing deadline, and continuously resident inside the city limits for the 12 months before that deadline. Whether it passed has not been confirmed.
records.charter_location: Article III. Sec. 3.01 Municipal elections, 3.02 Filing for office, 3.03 Official ballots, 3.04 Elections, 3.05 Oath of office. Candidate qualifications are Article II Sec. 2.04, with 2.05 Judge of qualifications.
records.has_changed: Yes. Measures A and E in 2021 and Proposition B in 2023 all touched election rules. Measure E replaced local ballot and election requirements with a pointer to state law.
records.why_it_matters: When a local election rule is replaced with a pointer to state law, the rule can change without a Copperas Cove vote.

records.name: City Council authority
records.what_is_it: The council is the elected body that passes ordinances, adopts the budget, sets the tax rate, and appoints and supervises the city manager.
records.charter_location: Article II. Sec. 2.01 through 2.12, including 2.06 Compensation, 2.09 Meetings of council, 2.10 Rules of procedure, 2.11 Investigative power of the council.
records.has_changed: Yes. Measure D in 2021 revised Sec. 2.09 on council meetings and deleted four other sections. Measure M replaced the local conflict of interest rule with the state standard. Pay increases were proposed and rejected in both 2021 and 2023.
records.why_it_matters: Council meeting rules decide when residents can show up and speak. Council pay is one of the few council matters residents get a direct vote on.

records.name: Mayor authority
records.what_is_it: In a council-manager city the mayor is usually a voting member of the council with ceremonial and presiding duties, rather than a chief executive. The exact role is set by the charter.
records.charter_location: Article II Sec. 2.03 Presiding officer: mayor and mayor pro tempore. Compensation is Sec. 2.06.
records.has_changed: Only mayoral compensation appears in the records we hold, proposed and rejected in 2021 and again in 2023.
records.why_it_matters: Residents often assume the mayor runs the city. In a council-manager city that is usually the city manager's job. The charter is what settles it.

records.name: City Manager authority
records.what_is_it: The city manager is the appointed chief administrator who runs city departments day to day. The city manager is not elected.
records.can_residents_do_it: Residents cannot hire or fire the city manager directly. Residents elect the council, and the council appoints and supervises the city manager.
records.charter_location: Article IV Administrative Services. Sec. 4.01 City manager, 4.02 Acting city manager, 4.03 Department heads, 4.04 Participation of city manager and other department heads in meetings.
records.has_changed: Measure H in 2021 would allow the city manager to miss a council meeting with council approval. Measure K moved the personnel plan from a five-year to an annual cycle. Measure M applied the state conflict of interest standard to city officials.
records.why_it_matters: The person with the most day to day authority over city operations is the one residents did not vote for. How that person is appointed, evaluated and removed is the whole question.

records.name: Vacancies and forfeiture of office
records.what_is_it: A vacancy happens when a council seat empties mid-term, through resignation, death, forfeiture or removal. The charter says how it gets filled.
records.can_residents_do_it: Whether residents get a special election or the council appoints a replacement depends on the charter. That section has not been obtained.
records.charter_location: Article II Sec. 2.07 Vacancies, forfeitures, filling of vacancies.
records.has_changed: Measure C in 2021 revised the requirements for holding a hearing on an alleged forfeiture of office.
records.why_it_matters: Forfeiture is a way a seat can empty without residents voting on it. Appointment is a way a seat can fill without residents voting on it. Both belong in the same conversation.

records.name: Debt and bonds
records.what_is_it: Cities borrow money in several different ways. Some kinds of borrowing require a public vote and some do not.
records.can_residents_do_it: Residents vote on general obligation bond propositions when they are called. Other borrowing methods under Texas law do not require an election, though some carry a petition right for residents.
records.charter_location: Article VII Issuance and Sale of Bonds. Sec. 7.01 Power to borrow. Sec. 7.02 is Reserved. Related: Article VIII Finance Administration.
records.has_changed: Measure I in 2021 moved the capital improvement plan review from every five years to annually.
records.why_it_matters: This is where most residents assume they have a vote and often do not. The specific borrowing instrument decides it, and the charter may or may not add a stricter local limit on top of state law.

records.name: Budget and tax authority
records.what_is_it: The budget is the city's annual spending plan. The tax rate is what funds much of it. The charter sets the process and the deadlines.
records.can_residents_do_it: Residents can speak at required public hearings. State law sets voter approval rate triggers for certain tax rate increases.
records.charter_location: Article VI The Budget. Sec. 6.01 Fiscal year, 6.02 Preparation and submission of proposed operating budget, 6.02.1 Amending the operating budget. Taxation is Article IX Sec. 9.01 Power to tax.
records.has_changed: Measures I, J and L in 2021 touched the capital improvement plan, the capital outlay plan and check countersigning. Measure E eliminated Sec. 10.09 on submission of annual reports.
records.why_it_matters: Budget deadlines and required reports are what let a resident see a decision coming before it is final.
